definition: Deride means to mock or laugh at with contempt.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word deride. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know deride should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Veteran deckhands deride the yacht club's white gloves and creased trousers every time the launch putters past.
Tease sits far below deride: tease laughs with its target — affection wearing a grin — while deride laughs at it, meaning to make it smaller.
Ridicule goes further than tease — the laughter turns public and pointed; deride claims the most: mockery with contempt in it, laughter meant to make its target smaller.

To scoff at something is to dismiss it with a quick sneering noise — derision in one syllable, usually aimed at an idea or a claim. Deride goes wider and louder: sustained mockery of a person or thing, with contempt carried in the laughter.

To mock is to make fun of something, often by imitating it — the exaggerated voice, the copied walk. Deride is blunter: open laughter aimed down at its target, with the contempt as the point. Mockery can be sly or theatrical; deride announces the scorn.

The 1896 etiquette guide gives lady cyclists a full chapter, and the tone is a sneer: it derides the bloomers, the posture, the "wheeled hoyden" herself, and advises gentlemen to keep their bows from any woman met astride a machine.
Derision, the chapter shows, needs no argument — contempt and a laugh will carry a page further than a fact.
Deride is the exact word for that chapter, because it means to mock or laugh at with contempt — both parts required.
Teasing laughs without the contempt; criticism judges without the laugh.
Derision is the laugh that means to shrink you.
Deride is face-out mockery — it happens in the open, and the contempt is the point.
Tease when the laugh is kind; ridicule when it is public but you want the contempt left unsaid.
Inside this unit: denigrate works behind the back, deprecate talks worth down without laughing, and deplore would never laugh at all.

In 1901 the editors of the county Gazette printed a standing joke: whenever news ran short, they sent a reporter to the Hollis brothers' barn for another story about the 'flying bicycle.' The brothers were easy to deride.
They were bicycle mechanics, not engineers; their machine was sewn from shirt cloth; and their test field was a cow pasture.
Columns held them up for open ridicule, and readers wrote in with jokes of their own — the laughter was public, sustained, and aimed squarely down.
Then, one gusty October morning, the machine cleared the fence line and stayed up for a full minute.
The Gazette buried the item on page six.
Years later the surviving editor admitted the paper had never really weighed the brothers' claims at all — it had simply enjoyed laughing at them, and the habit had cost it the story of the century.
